contentBlocks.text: The Stellar Story: What Does "Subaru" Actually Mean?

In Japanese, “Subaru” (スバル) means “unite” or “gather together.” It’s a nice, low-key name that gets right to the brand’s heart—harmony and connection. But most people, don’t know there’s a starry backstory to it, too.

The name wasn’t picked by chance—it’s a shout-out to the Pleiades star cluster, the group of stars that’s fascinated people for thousands of years. The Greeks called them Atlas’ seven daughters, but in Japan, they’ve always stood for unity. When Subaru’s predecessor got its start, “Subaru” wasn’t just a pretty name—it was a promise. It marked the coming together of five specific Japanese companies—Fuji Kogyo, Fuji Jidosha, Omiya Fuji Kogyo, Utsunomiya Sharyo, and Tokyo Fuji Sangyo—into one tight, engineering-focused team, which would later become Fuji Heavy Industries (now Subaru Corporation).
Decoding the Badge: Why Six Stars?
You’ve seen that blue-and-silver oval on the back of countless Outbacks and WRXs, but it’s more than just a pretty design. It’s a literal map of the company’s history.
The Pleiades Connection

The stars in the logo are a direct nod to the Pleiades cluster in the Taurus constellation. In Japan, these stars are "Subaru." By putting them on the grille, the brand isn't just showing off its Japanese heritage—it’s grounding its identity in the stars.
The "Missing" Seventh Star

Wait, aren't the Pleiades known as the "Seven Sisters"? Look closely at the logo and you’ll only count six. There’s a clever bit of realism here: only six stars in the cluster are typically visible to the naked eye. But more importantly, the six stars symbolize the six companies that merged back in the 1950s to form Fuji Heavy Industries (now Subaru Corporation). One large star represents the parent company, while the five smaller stars represent the firms that joined forces under it.

Subaru Logo Timeline

The original badge wasn't just a logo; it was a statement. Subaru kicked things off with a raw, three-dimensional representation of the Taurus constellation. They used a heavy silver metallic sheen and sharp shadows to give it some serious "depth," framing the stars in an oval that felt like a window into deep space. It was bold, industrial, and meant to show that this new team was ready to build something substantial.

As the iconic Subaru 360 began to hit the streets, the badge went gold. They elongated the stars and stretched the connecting beams to create a wider, more dramatic horizontal "stretch." The oval frame was thinned out, making the stars—with their new, sharp protruding edges—the undisputed heroes of the grille. This is the "vintage gold" look that collectors still obsess over today.

By '59, Subaru decided it was time for some color. They dropped the gold in favor of a high-contrast silver-on-red scheme. Why red? To signal a brand in motion. It was aggressive, high-energy, and designed to pop against the chrome of 1950s and 60s car design, reflecting a young company’s hunger for progress.

The 70s brought a massive vibe shift. Subaru ditched the red and introduced a deep navy blue, finally giving the stars their natural home: the night sky. They experimented with a unique "U-shaped" housing with a flat bottom—a look that felt very "of its time." For the first time, the stars started to break free, with their points actually protruding past the edges of the oval frame.

In 1980, the logo grew up. Designers added a bold black outline to the silver stars to give them more "pop" and a professional, crisp finish. They finally did away with the connecting lines between the stars, letting the shapes speak for themselves. The frame became a sophisticated sandwich of white, gray, and black, making the badge look less like a toy and more like a precision instrument.

Later that same year, Subaru pulled the trigger on a major cleanup. They repositioned the stars and completely streamlined the composition. This was the "Aha!" moment where the logo finally started looking like the one we recognize today—cleaner, more balanced, and much more "corporate" in the best way possible.

As we hit the new millennium, Subaru went "Premium." The badge transitioned into a sleek, modern emblem with a heavy chrome border. The stars moved into a tighter geometric pattern, featuring razor-sharp edges and a high-gloss 3D effect. This was also when the "SUBARU" wordmark became a permanent fixture below the oval, rendered in a bold, silver-capped font that screamed Y2K-era tech.

Subaru didn’t reinvent the wheel in '03; they just polished it to perfection. The blue background was deepened to a rich, "midnight" navy, and the star outlines were beefed up for better visibility. Everything felt a bit more muscular—the oval was more pronounced, and the shading was more sophisticated. It was a subtle flex of brand maturity.

The current badge is all about the "Sleek & Tech" look. Subaru swapped the heavy navy for a lighter, more vibrant azure hue and transitioned the grays into a bright, clean silver. The overall ellipse is now narrower and longer, giving the badge a more aerodynamic, "fast" appearance. By recoloring the brand lettering in a subtle dark gray, they finally achieved a harmonious, cohesive look where the name and the stars feel like one single, seamless unit.
